title: Chicago's Tax Increment Financing: Who Paid, Who Gained? (González, Wilson, Córdova & Campos, UIC Great Cities Institute, Aug 26 2026)
what_was_fetched: News-story landing page fetched directly (curl, browser UA, HTTP 200); it links a Box-hosted PDF of the full 108-page report (uofi.box.com/s/yzd8d2qz6amqybiz6ubxs9rfoxzjwvkr), which was also fetched directly (13.6MB, 108 pp.) and parsed in full with pymupdf. Saved locally at scratchpad/t0-2026-09-25/GCI_TIF_Report_Digital.pdf and gci_tif_report_full.txt. Full text read, including Executive Summary, Section 2 (TIF Impact on Property Values and Taxes), Appendix B (Methodology), and the Policy Recommendations section. Also read the landing page's own 'Media Coverage' block, which includes a direct author (Matthew D. Wilson) rebuttal to a methodological caution raised by William Fulton (UC San Diego) in the New York Times' coverage.
verdict: NEW research/ page (a Core-tier, university-institute empirical report on this scale warrants its own dedicated entry per the Scan Depth policy) + ENRICH places/chicago.md (a new, dated, empirical TIF section distinct from the existing Hoyt/land-cycle material) + ENRICH concepts/land-value-capture.md (its TIF-in-practice material, alongside the existing San Antonio TIRZ and Wisconsin levy-limit case studies, as a third, sharpest, and largest-scale TIF critique).
claim_grade: B-claim (peer-institutional empirical report with disclosed quasi-experimental method), Tier 1 (UIC Great Cities Institute — a university research institute per EDITORIAL §4c).
content_summary: 40+ year (1984-2025) audit of Chicago TIF using a parcel panel (~750,000 parcels/year, 2010-2024, Cook County Assessor Parcel Universe + Assessed Values datasets) matched to a sample of 346 TIF-funded projects (2000-2020, City of Chicago TIF project data, routine-maintenance and <$1M projects excluded). Key figures, all page-cited in the extracted text: (1) TIF districts generated approximately $16.6 billion in revenue 1984-2025 (nominal; inflation-adjusted >$22bn), across 184 districts created, 108 active in 2024 (p.10/'Executive Summary'). (2) Over 2014-2023, TIF raised citywide property tax rates by an average of 13.7% (rising from 7.8% in 2014 to 18.6% in 2023) -- NOTE: the report's own author rebuttal on the same page states a DIFFERENT, higher '17 to 19 percent' figure for the tax-rate effect specifically 'in 2023' across all four of the report's robustness scenarios; the 13.7%/18.6% figures are the headline single-scenario numbers from the report body itself (Section 2, p.~38-39) -- this translates to ~$721M/year in additional taxes, ~$1.1bn in 2023, $7.21bn cumulative 2014-2023, or $878/year ($6,616 over the decade) for a typical $300,000 home. (3) Only 1.8% of the citywide EAV increment within TIF districts is attributable to TIF investment itself (the 'but-for' causal estimate); the remaining 98.2% is 'organic growth' (inflation and market appreciation that would have occurred regardless). The report states this is its PREFERRED estimate among four scenarios tested (a null-effect scenario through a deliberately pro-TIF scenario), under which the TIF-attributable share rises only to about 6%; the tax-shift finding ($1bn+/year, in every scenario) is stated to be far more robust across scenarios than the exact 1.8% figure. (4) 51% of tracked TIF project spending since 1986 went to downtown or adjacent neighborhoods (Executive Summary; GCI's own tracking, not a share of all TIF revenue). (5) Methodology: difference-in-differences / matched-parcel design -- each property is compared with its OWN prior values over time (not cross-sectionally assumed identical to comparison parcels), testing PARALLEL PRE-TREATMENT TRENDS between TIF-project-adjacent parcels and parcels a half-mile to a mile away, for every property type, before attributing any post-treatment divergence to TIF. This directly answers a published NYT-reported methodological caution from William Fulton (UC San Diego) that the study assumed treated/control parcels were 'exactly the same' -- the report's own co-author states this characterization is inaccurate given the pre-trend-testing design. Recommendations (Section on Policy Recommendations, p.89-90): (a) amend state TIF law to reduce diversions from overlapping taxing districts, especially school districts (e.g. mandatory inflation-adjustment of frozen EAV, or the 'transit TIF' revenue-sharing model applied to all new districts); (b) more aggressively phase out downtown TIFs that have achieved their original goals (naming LaSalle Central TIF, $1.4bn+ captured since 2006, scheduled to expire 2030, recommends against extension); (c) substantially increase TIF assistance to small business/neighborhood/workforce programs (currently <2% of four decades of spending); (d) overhaul the city's TIF data reporting (called a 'confusing hodgepodge' of ~200 datasets); (e) create independent oversight (an Office of Financial Analysis expansion or a NYC-IBO-style independent budget office); (f) expand affordable-housing TIF subsidies while controlling mushrooming per-unit ('soft') costs. Report explicitly does not recommend eliminating TIF outright.
existing_wiki_coverage: places/chicago.md currently covers ONLY Homer Hoyt's 1830-1933 land-value-cycle study and Gaffney's separate 1890s growth-and-politics case; it has no TIF content at all -- this is a genuinely new topical layer for the page, not a duplicate. concepts/land-value-capture.md already carries two 2026 US TIF case studies (San Antonio's TIRZ system and Wisconsin's levy-limit interaction) with the same 'TIF captures value but where it goes/how it interacts with other levies is a distributional design choice' framing this report reinforces at much larger scale and with a stronger causal design (parcel panel + pre-trend testing vs. the San Antonio/Wisconsin pieces' journalistic sourcing). No existing wiki page currently states a 'TIF causal attribution' percentage (the 1.8%/98.2% split) or a citywide tax-rate-shift percentage for any US city; this would be the wiki's first source doing so with an explicit counterfactual method.
uncertainties: (1) The Executive Summary's headline 13.7%/18.6% tax-rate-shift figures and the author-rebuttal's '17 to 19 percent... under every scenario' figure are NOT the same number -- a T1 should resolve exactly what these two figures each measure (average-over-period vs. terminal-year-2023-across-scenarios) before publishing either headline figure, and should quote both with their precise definitions rather than picking one. (2) The report is Tier 1 institutionally but is University-authored advocacy-adjacent research responding directly to public controversy over Mayor Brandon Johnson's TIF reforms; it has already drawn a published counter-argument (Crain's Chicago Business, Greg Hinz, 'The case against Chicago TIFs leaves out one inconvenient fact. They worked.') that a T1 should read before writing a page, to keep the wiki's treatment balanced rather than one-sided -- this counter-view was not fetched in this pass (link known: listed in the landing page's Media Coverage block) and needs its own access attempt. (3) I did not independently verify the report's underlying Cook County Assessor data or replicate the but-for model; the 1.8%/13.7%/51%/$16.6bn figures are as stated in the report's own Executive Summary and Section 2/5, not independently re-derived here.

title: Land, the Wealth We Can Actually Tax: California's land, the proposed Billionaire Wealth Tax, and a better way to fund the state's future (Lars Doucet & Greg Miller, Center for Land Economics)
what_was_fetched: Full report page fetched directly (curl, browser UA, HTTP 200, ~41.5K words of extracted text) -- the page itself carries the ENTIRE report body (not just an abstract/landing page), through all seven sections (Overview through 'A Better Play'). A separate PDF version is also linked (reports.landeconomics.org/reports/california-wealth-tax.pdf) but was not additionally fetched since the HTML page's text is already the full report. NOTE: the page itself is dated 'June 2026,' not the September 2026 the queue context gave -- this should be corrected before publishing (the report predates the queue's discovery, or the discovery date and publication date differ; a T1 should re-check the page's own date stamp).
verdict: NEW places/california.md (no California place page currently exists on the wiki; the corpus digest and repo confirm this, and this report alone is enough Tier-1-adjacent, transparently-methoded material -- plus the wiki's separate California irrigation-districts and mass-appraisal-methods pages -- to justify a jurisdiction profile). The report itself is cited throughout as the PROPONENT'S OWN triangulated estimate, per EDITORIAL §4c (Center for Land Economics, Greg Miller and Lars Doucet, are explicitly Tier 2 in sources/audit/people-tiers.json), never as independent confirmation that California's land is undertaxed.
claim_grade: B-claim (an original empirical estimate with fully disclosed method and named data sources), Tier 2 (Center for Land Economics / Doucet & Miller — advocacy-institute proponent estimate per people-tiers.json; cite as origin/proponent only, never as support that the LVT proposal is correct).
content_summary: Core empirical claim: California's total land value is $8.14 trillion (the report's own headline figure), triangulated three ways, all converging: (1) CLE's own parcel-level pipeline ($8.14tn) -- Regrid parcel data joined to CA county assessor records, at the level of (census tract x property category): step 1 estimates market value from actual 2023-2026 sales (median price/sqft for improved parcels, trimmed 5% each tail; price/acre binned by lot size for vacant land); step 2 extracts a land-share ratio from the assessor's land/total split on each recently-sold parcel (immune to Prop 13's absolute-value distortion because it uses a RATIO, not the assessor's stale absolute land value) and applies it to the market-value estimate; step 3 sums across all buckets statewide. (2) FHFA per-acre residential land-value rates by census tract (2024 release, Working Paper 19-01), joined to CA parcels: $8.76tn -- independently derived, converges closely. (3) Time-trended historical sales (every historical sale in the dataset, price-indexed forward by county-and-category): $10.12tn -- the highest of the three. For comparison, the NAIVE approach of simply summing the assessor's own reported 'land value' column gives $3.96tn, which the report explicitly rejects as artificially depressed by Prop 13's 1976-frozen, sale-triggered-reset assessment regime. The California parcel data sources named: Regrid (parcel records), CA county assessor records, FHFA (Federal Housing Finance Agency, 2024 release), FRED (CASTHPI house-price index, CPIAUCSL), US Census ACS B25038 (homeowner tenure duration, for the Prop-13-gap cohort-weighting estimate). Three explicitly STATED, self-disclosed conservative biases, all pushing the $8.14tn estimate DOWN: (a) the sales lookback window (Jan 2023-Jan 2026) uses the MEDIAN price in that window rather than the most recent, understating a rising market; (b) the land-share ratio is taken from recently-sold (disproportionately newer-construction) parcels and applied to the whole parcel universe, understating land share for older unsold properties; (c) tribal, federal, state, county, school-district, conservation and timeshare parcels are EXCLUDED entirely from the total (real land value, unmeasured). The report states '$8.14T should be read as a floor... the true number almost certainly higher.' The $20bn/yr comparison: California's proposed Billionaire Wealth Tax (BWT) is a 5% one-time levy on ~200 CA billionaires, payable over 5 years, targeting $100bn total ($20bn/yr), built on a $2 trillion taxable base and 1% annual rate per the BWT's own supporting expert report by Galle, Gamage, Saez & Shanske ('GGSS'). NOTE: the CLE report does NOT name a specific bill/ballot-measure number for the BWT anywhere in the fetched text -- only the informal name 'Billionaire Wealth Tax' is used throughout; a T1 should independently identify and cite the actual legislative or ballot-measure text if the wiki writes this up, since the CLE report itself does not supply that citation. The report's central policy claim: a 0.25% LVT on its own $8.14tn estimate (or 0.2% on the higher $10.12tn time-trended estimate) raises the same $20bn/year the BWT promises -- versus needing ~1.6-1.9% on the BWT's own (CLE-recalculated) eroded ~$1.0-1.27tn realistic base, because CLE separately argues (citing a paper by Jaros, Rauh et al.) that ~$0.95tn (47%) of the BWT's assumed $2tn base has already left California via pre-2026 billionaire relocations (Page, Brin, Thiel, Hankey, Kalanick, Spielberg, ~$540bn combined) plus a Zuckerberg move (~$220bn) plus a separate $200bn Jaros-Rauh-identified GGSS overestimate. Tier 1 sources the report itself leans on: FHFA (federal agency data), Oates & Schwab (1997) Pittsburgh study (already Tier 1 confirmed on this wiki), Stiglitz's Henry George Theorem paper (Tier 1), the California Legislative Analyst's Office 2016 Prop 13 report (official state body), and a Berkeley Institute for Young Americans (2023) parcel-level Prop 13 study (university-affiliated research institute -- standing not yet assessed against people-tiers.json, worth a T1 check). Saez (of GGSS) is separately Tier 1 confirmed on this wiki; Galle, Gamage and Shanske's academic standing was not independently checked in this pass.
existing_wiki_coverage: No California place page exists. concepts/land-value-capture.md and economic-rent.md carry other US land-value estimates (Larson/BEA $23tn national figure, Doucet's Land Is a Big Deal compilation) but nothing California-specific. No existing wiki page discusses Prop 13's assessment-gap mechanics in any depth. The Billionaire Wealth Tax and its GGSS expert-report backing are not mentioned anywhere on the wiki currently.
uncertainties: (1) The page's own 'June 2026' date vs. the queue's 'September 2026' framing needs reconciling before publication -- check for a later-dated revision or whether the queue simply mis-dated discovery. (2) This is a Tier 2 advocacy report defending an LVT-favorable policy conclusion against a rival tax proposal it has an institutional stake in opposing; a T1 should look for independent (Tier 1) commentary on the $8.14tn estimate or the BWT's own erosion critique before treating either as settled, and should keep the whole 'BWT is critically flawed' framing attributed to CLE rather than stated as the wiki's own assessment. (3) The report cites Jaros, Rauh et al. for the billionaire-departure and $200bn-overestimate figures -- this looks like it could itself be a citable academic paper (Rauh is a Stanford finance professor, a plausible Tier 1 name) but the full citation (venue, year, title) was not visible in the fetched text and should be tracked down directly rather than taken at CLE's paraphrase. (4) The 'median residential parcel... land value approximately $425,000... 0.25% LVT... approximately $850/year' pocketbook figures are CLE's own downstream arithmetic on its own estimate, not a separately sourced claim.

title: What Capital Never Told You About Rent (Michael Garfield with Simon Quarmby, Humans on the Loop / Atlas Research Group blog, 22 Sep 2026)
what_was_fetched: Full essay fetched directly (curl, browser UA, HTTP 200) and read in full, including reader comments.

claim_grade: D-claim (interpretive/argumentative essay, no original empirical content), Tier 2 (newsletter/blog essay by practitioner-authors, per EDITORIAL §4c) -- origin/proponent only if ever cited, never as support.
content_summary: Argues rent (not profit) built the modern economy, tracing English enclosure (12th-19th c.) through interest, IP, platforms, and a forecast 'Total Rent' endpoint in metered AI/compute access. Quotes Keynes's 'euthanasia of the rentier' (already on rentier.md, verbatim, sourced to the primary Ch. 24 text there) and references Ricardo, Mill and George's 1879 'unearned income' coinage (all already extensively covered). Two potentially NEW Tier 1 leads surfaced by the essay, NOT currently on the wiki (checked by grep across the full repo): (1) Michael Heller & Rebecca S. Eisenberg's 'anticommons' concept (fragmented IP ownership creating a 'patent thicket' that blocks downstream innovation) -- this is a real, citable, established academic concept (Heller, Columbia Law; Eisenberg, Michigan Law; the primary paper is Heller & Eisenberg, 'Can Patents Deter Innovation? The Anticommons in Biomedical Research,' Science, 1998), referenced only in passing and unsourced-to-a-specific-paper in this essay -- a T1 wanting to pursue it would need to find and read the primary Science paper directly, not cite this essay for it. (2) Yochai Benkler (Harvard Law) quoted on commons-dependent market economies -- also a real Tier 1 academic (The Wealth of Networks), also unsourced to a specific work in this essay. Neither concept is used by the essay in a way that adds empirical weight to the wiki's existing rent-extraction case; both would need independent primary-source verification before any use, and neither is really about LAND rent (they're IP/commons-governance concepts, tangential to this wiki's core scope, though within the ALL-rents mission per EDITORIAL's mission statement).
